title: Meet the Character
objectives: I can use ten words to tell how a character feels, acts, and treats others.
I can use clues in a story to choose the best word for a character.
I can find the endings -ful, -ous, and -y in describing words.
I can write about two characters who are different from each other.
rationale: Third graders can already feel these traits in characters, but they often fall back on 'nice' and 'mean'. This opening unit gives them ten precise words that sort into how a character feels (timid, bashful, gloomy, cranky), how a character plays tricks or moves (mischievous, sly, clumsy), and how a character treats other people (boastful, courteous, obedient). Naming a trait and proving it with an action is the first step toward character analysis in later grades. Three of the words end in -ous or -ful, so the unit also plants early awareness of suffixes before the affix units later in the year.

words.def: Shy and easily frightened; not brave.
words.ex: The timid kitten hid under the bed when the doorbell rang.
words.ex2: On his first day at school, Ravi felt timid and sat quietly near the door.
words.nonExample: A child who runs up and greets everyone with a big wave is not timid.

apps.academic: A timid character in a story often learns to be braver by the end.
apps.spoken: I was timid at first, but then I joined the game.
apps.writing: Use timid to show a character who is afraid to speak or to move.

cloze.s: The ___ mouse peeked out of its hole, then dashed back inside at the tiniest noise.

cloze2.s: Too ___ to raise her hand, Ana whispered her answer to the girl beside her.

misuse.s: The timid boy marched onto the stage and sang loudly without any fear.
misuse.why: A timid person is shy and afraid; this boy shows no fear at all.

visual.alt: A small mouse peeking out of a hole with wide, scared eyes.

words.def: Dark and sad; not cheerful or bright.
words.ex: The gloomy hallway had no windows and smelled like old rain.
words.ex2: After his team lost, Theo felt gloomy for the rest of the day.
words.nonExample: A bright, sunny room full of laughing friends is not gloomy.

apps.academic: A gloomy setting can make readers feel worried or sad.
apps.spoken: It is such a gloomy morning with all this rain.
apps.writing: Use gloomy for both a sad mood and a dark, rainy place.

cloze.s: The ___ sky filled with dark clouds, and the whole town stayed indoors.

cloze2.s: Pablo wore a ___ face all afternoon because he had lost his favorite toy.

misuse.s: It was a gloomy day, so we all danced and cheered in the bright sunshine.
misuse.why: Gloomy means dark and sad; dancing in bright sunshine is the opposite.

visual.alt: A sad child looking out a window at gray rain clouds.

words.def: Playful in a naughty way, often causing small trouble.
words.ex: The mischievous monkey grabbed a visitor's hat and ran up a tree.
words.ex2: A mischievous grin spread across Jo's face as she hid the teacher's pen.
words.nonExample: A student who sits quietly and follows every rule is not mischievous.
words.rel: how a character plays tricks or moves

apps.academic: A mischievous character often starts the trouble that a story has to solve.
apps.spoken: My little brother is so mischievous that he hid my shoes.
apps.writing: Use mischievous for playful tricks that are naughty but not truly mean.

cloze.s: The ___ puppy pulled the socks out of the laundry basket and ran around the yard with them.

cloze2.s: With a ___ giggle, the twins swapped the labels on two jars of paint.

misuse.s: The mischievous girl never played a single trick and always did exactly what the rules said.
misuse.why: Mischievous means playful and naughty; following every rule is the opposite.

visual.alt: A monkey wearing a borrowed hat and grinning.

words.def: Easily embarrassed and shy around other people.
words.ex: The bashful boy blushed when the whole class sang to him.
words.ex2: She gave a bashful smile and hid behind her mother's arm.
words.nonExample: A child who loves being the center of attention is not bashful.

apps.academic: A bashful character may blush or look down when others pay attention.
apps.spoken: I get bashful when people clap for me.
apps.writing: Use bashful to show a shy feeling that comes from being looked at.

cloze.s: The ___ girl looked at her shoes and answered in a tiny voice when the visitor said hello.

cloze2.s: He felt ___ when everyone clapped, so his cheeks turned pink and he looked away.

misuse.s: The bashful singer shouted, "Look at me!" and danced in front of the whole crowd.
misuse.why: Bashful means shy about being noticed; shouting for attention is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child with pink cheeks covering their eyes with one hand.

words.def: Grumpy and easily annoyed, often because you are tired.
words.ex: The cranky baby cried until she finally fell asleep.
words.ex2: Dad gets cranky when he has to wait in a long line.
words.nonExample: A person who is calm and smiling after a long trip is not cranky.

apps.academic: A cranky character may snap at others because of tiredness or hunger.
apps.spoken: I'm cranky because I did not sleep well.
apps.writing: Use cranky to explain a bad mood that has a small, clear cause.

cloze.s: After missing his nap, the ___ toddler pushed away his lunch and cried.

cloze2.s: Everyone felt ___ after the long, hot bus ride with no snacks.

misuse.s: She was cranky, so she hummed a happy song and gave everyone a hug.
misuse.why: Cranky means grumpy; humming and hugging show a good mood.

visual.alt: A tired, frowning child rubbing their eyes.

words.def: Clever in a secret or tricky way.
words.ex: The sly fox waited until the farmer looked away.
words.ex2: With a sly wink, Marta slipped the last cookie into her pocket.
words.nonExample: A girl who tells the truth and shares her plans out loud is not sly.
words.rel: how a character plays tricks or moves

apps.academic: A sly character in a folktale often wins by tricking someone.
apps.spoken: He gave me a sly smile, and I knew he had a secret.
apps.writing: Use sly for a clever plan that someone keeps hidden.

cloze.s: The ___ cat pretended to sleep while it watched the goldfish bowl.

cloze2.s: With a ___ smile, Kito hid the key behind his back and said he had no idea where it was.

misuse.s: The sly thief shouted his plan to the whole town before he began.
misuse.why: Sly means secretly clever; shouting a plan out loud is not sly.

visual.alt: A fox peeking around a corner with narrowed eyes.

words.def: Not careful or smooth when moving; often tripping or dropping things.
words.ex: The clumsy waiter dropped his tray and spilled juice everywhere.
words.ex2: Ben felt clumsy in his big new boots and tripped on the first step.
words.nonExample: A dancer who glides across the floor without a stumble is not clumsy.
words.rel: how a character plays tricks or moves

apps.academic: A clumsy character's accidents can cause funny or serious problems in a story.
apps.spoken: I'm so clumsy today; I keep dropping things.
apps.writing: Use clumsy with a picture of what happened, such as tripping or spilling.

cloze.s: The ___ puppy tripped over its own paws and rolled down the grassy hill.

cloze2.s: Carlos was so ___ that he bumped into three desks on his way to the door.

misuse.s: The clumsy juggler never dropped a ball and moved as smoothly as water.
misuse.why: Clumsy means awkward and often dropping things; moving smoothly is the opposite.

visual.alt: A puppy tumbling head over paws on the grass.

words.def: Talking too proudly about what you have or can do.
words.ex: The boastful runner told everyone he would win the race by a mile.
words.ex2: Nobody enjoyed Kyle's boastful stories about his new video game.
words.nonExample: A kid who says "Good game!" to the other team is not boastful.
words.rel: how a character treats other people

apps.academic: A boastful character often learns a lesson when the bragging goes wrong.
apps.spoken: I don't want to sound boastful, but I finished first.
apps.writing: Use boastful for someone who brags more than is kind.

cloze.s: The ___ boy kept telling everyone that his bike was the fastest in the whole town.

cloze2.s: Her ___ words about winning every game made her teammates roll their eyes.

misuse.s: The boastful girl never mentioned her trophy and quietly thanked her team.
misuse.why: Boastful means bragging; staying quiet and thanking others is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child holding a trophy high and shouting through cupped hands.

words.def: Polite and respectful in the way you treat others.
words.ex: The courteous boy held the door open for the whole line.
words.ex2: Nia was courteous to the new student and showed him around the school.
words.nonExample: Pushing past people without saying "excuse me" is not courteous.
words.rel: how a character treats other people

apps.academic: A courteous character uses polite words and actions, even with someone who is upset.
apps.spoken: Thank you for being so courteous to my grandmother.
apps.writing: Use courteous to praise polite words or actions, such as holding a door.

cloze.s: The ___ clerk smiled, said thank you, and helped the customer carry her bags.

cloze2.s: In a ___ voice, the guest asked if he could please borrow a pen.

misuse.s: The courteous boy shoved past everyone and yelled at the teacher.
misuse.why: Courteous means polite; shoving and yelling are rude.

visual.alt: A child holding a door open for a smiling classmate.

words.def: Doing what you are told to do by someone in charge.
words.ex: The obedient dog sat down the moment his owner raised a hand.
words.ex2: Obedient students lined up quietly when the bell rang.
words.nonExample: A child who ignores the rules and runs off is not obedient.
words.rel: how a character treats other people

apps.academic: An obedient character follows instructions from a parent, teacher, or leader.
apps.spoken: My dog is very obedient and always comes when I call.
apps.writing: Use obedient for someone who follows rules or directions.

cloze.s: The ___ puppy waited by the door until his owner said, "Let's go."

cloze2.s: She was so ___ that she cleaned her room as soon as her mom asked.

misuse.s: The obedient boy ignored every rule and did the opposite of what his teacher asked.
misuse.why: Obedient means following directions; ignoring rules is the opposite.

visual.alt: A dog sitting calmly while a hand is raised in front of it.

passage.title: The Class Pet Show
paras: On Friday, Room 12 held a pet show. Mina stood by the door with her small turtle in her hands. She was timid, and she hoped no one would call her name. Her friend Leo was bashful too, and his cheeks turned pink whenever someone looked his way.

Drew arrived next. He was boastful. "My dog is the smartest dog in the world," he said loudly, "and the fastest and the best." Just then his clumsy puppy tripped on the rug and knocked a basket of crayons onto the floor. Drew's face turned red.

Sara's dog, Biscuit, was obedient. He sat, shook hands, and waited when she said "stay." A mischievous gray cat named Pepper watched from the bookshelf. She gave a sly look at the crayons, hopped down, and rolled one across the floor.
Mr. Grant was a little cranky that morning because the day was gloomy and rain tapped on the windows. But he took a deep breath and said in a calm voice, "Let's pick up the crayons together."

The judge, Ms. Patel, was courteous to every child. She thanked Mina for her patience and asked about the turtle. Mina smiled and spoke clearly. For the first time that day, she did not feel timid at all.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "boastful" tells us that Drew
choices: bragged about his dog
felt shy about his dog
was kind to the other children
forgot his dog at home
qs.why: Drew says his dog is the smartest, fastest, and best, which is bragging.

qs.q: Why did Drew's face turn red?
choices: He was angry that Mina had a turtle.
He was cold from the rain outside.
He wanted to sing for the class.
He bragged about his puppy, and then the puppy made a mess.
qs.why: Drew had just bragged, so the puppy tripping and spilling crayons embarrassed him.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Biscuit was obedient?
choices: He sat near the gray cat.
He waited when Sara said "stay."
He belonged to a girl named Sara.
He rolled a crayon across the floor.
qs.why: Obedient means following directions, and waiting when told to stay is following a direction.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea of the passage?
choices: Pets should always stay at home.
At a pet show, the children and animals showed many kinds of personalities.
Rain is the worst kind of weather.
A turtle can win any contest.
qs.why: The passage describes different children and animals and how each one acts.

argue.prompt: Claim: Being courteous is the most important trait for a classmate. Do you agree or disagree? Give two reasons.
argue.frame: I agree (or disagree) that ___ because ___. Another reason is ___.

constructed.prompt: Write two sentences about two kids at a party, one timid and one boastful. Show each trait with an action.
look: gives one action for each trait
shows how the two kids are different
constructed.model: Ravi was timid and stood by the wall holding his cup. Marco was boastful and told everyone he had won every game.

constructed.prompt: A classmate is cranky and rude to you. Write what a courteous person might say or do, and explain why.
look: gives a polite and kind response
constructed.model: A courteous person would say, "You seem tired. Do you want to sit down?" That is kind even when the other person is cranky.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for personality and behavior, use them to analyze characters in a short narrative, notice the endings -ful, -ous, and -y, and write about two characters who are different. The routine is always the same: name the trait, then prove it with an action.

notes.va.timid.adj: Timid means easily scared or shy. Ask students what a timid character does with her voice and her body. Contrast with bold on a two-column chart.
notes.va.gloomy.adj: Gloomy works for places and for feelings. Model gloom + -y. Ask students to name a gloomy and a cheerful picture from a book they know.
notes.va.mischievous.adj: Mischievous is playful trouble, not cruelty. Show mischief + -ous and the f to v change. Ask what the difference is between a mischievous joke and a mean one.
notes.va.bashful.adj: Bashful and timid overlap. Timid is afraid; bashful is shy about being looked at. Have students act out a bashful face without words.
notes.va.cranky.adj: Cranky usually has a small cause such as hunger or tiredness. Ask students for a cause and a result: 'He was tired, so he was cranky.'
notes.va.sly.adj: Sly is cleverness that is hidden, so it often goes with a trick. Point out that sly is not always evil; a sly puzzle-maker can be fun.
notes.va.clumsy.adj: Clumsy describes moving, not thinking. Say that a clumsy person can be very smart. Invite students to act out a clumsy walk, then a smooth one.
notes.va.boastful.adj: Boastful is bragging that goes past being proud. Show boast + -ful. Ask students whether feeling proud and being boastful are the same.
notes.va.courteous.adj: Courteous is a more formal word for polite. Have students list courteous actions (hold a door, say please) rather than just the word.
notes.va.obedient.adj: Obedient is not the same as good or smart. Ask students about a time following directions kept someone safe, and a time to ask a question first.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The story says Drew told everyone his dog was the best, loudly. That is bragging, so boastful fits. Then his puppy tripped. I can prove clumsy with that action. When I pick a word for a character, I look for an action that shows it.'
discuss: Which character in a book you know is sly? What does the character do that shows it?
How can a person be both timid and courteous?
misconceptions: Timid and bashful mean exactly the same thing.
A boastful person is the same as a proud person.
extend: Draw a character and label three of the words from the unit next to the picture.
Rewrite a short scene so a timid character becomes bold, and tell which actions change.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the opposite pairs (timid and bold, gloomy and cheerful, boastful and modest) two days later and again after a week. Ask students to use one unit word whenever they describe a character in the next unit.

wida.oral: Partner A acts like a character from the unit without speaking. Partner B guesses the word and says one action that proves it.
